mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes heat from work as modes of energy transfer?

options.A: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, while work is energy transferred when a macroscopic force acts through a distance.
options.B: Heat is energy transferred when a macroscopic force acts through a distance, while work is energy transferred due to a temperature difference.
options.C: Both heat and work are transferred only when there is a change in the internal energy of a system.
options.D: Heat and work are identical concepts; the terms are used interchangeably in thermodynamics.

mcqs.answer: Heat is energy transferred due to a temperature difference, while work is energy transferred when a macroscopic force acts through a distance.
mcqs.explanation: Heat refers to energy that moves because of a temperature gradient between the system and its surroundings. Work refers to energy transferred when an external force moves the system's boundary (e.g., piston moving). Option A captures this distinction. Option B reverses the definitions, C confuses transfer with internal energy change, and D is false because heat and work are distinct modes of energy transfer.

mcqs.question: According to the sign convention used in NCERT physics for thermodynamic processes, if 500 J of work is done by the system and 200 J of heat is added to the system, what is the change in the internal energy of the system?
mcqs.explanation: NCERT physics adopts the sign convention ΔU = Q – W, where Q is heat added to the system (positive) and W is work done by the system (positive). Here Q = +200 J and W = +500 J, so ΔU = 200 J – 500 J = –300 J. The internal energy decreases by 300 J. Options A, C, and D result from incorrect application of the sign rule.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate work in simple thermodynamic processes
mcqs.question: A 1 mol ideal gas expands from 1 L to 3 L at 300 K. In process (i) the expansion is carried out isothermally and reversibly; in process (ii) the expansion occurs at constant external pressure of 1 atm (isobaric). Which process results in a larger magnitude of work done by the gas?

options.A: The isobaric process does more work.
options.B: The isothermal reversible process does more work.
options.C: Both processes do the same amount of work.
options.D: The work cannot be compared without knowing the heat capacity of the gas.

mcqs.answer: The isothermal reversible process does more work.
mcqs.explanation: For the isobaric (constant‑pressure) expansion: W = PΔV = (1 atm)(3 L – 1 L) = 2 L·atm = 2 × 101.3 J ≈ 202.6 J. For the reversible isothermal expansion of 1 mol ideal gas: W = nRT ln(Vf/Vi) = (1 mol)(8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)(300 K) ln(3) ≈ 2494 J × 1.0986 ≈ 2738 J. Hence the isothermal reversible process does far more work. Option B is correct; the other options either reverse the comparison or claim insufficient information, which is not true.

mcqs.question: In the pressure‑volume (P‑V) diagram described below, the system follows a rectangular cycle: (1) isobaric expansion from (P₁ = 2 atm, V₁ = 1 L) to (P₁, V₂ = 3 L); (2) isochoric heating to (P₂ = 1 atm, V₂); (3) isobaric compression back to (P₂, V₁); (4) isochoric cooling to the initial state. What is the net work done by the system in one complete cycle?
mcqs.explanation: The net work in a cyclic P‑V process equals the area enclosed by the loop. The rectangle has height |P₁ – P₂| = |2 atm – 1 atm| = 1 atm and width |V₂ – V₁| = 3 L – 1 L = 2 L. Area = 1 atm × 2 L = 2 L·atm. Converting to joules (1 L·atm = 101.3 J) gives 2 × 101.3 J ≈ 202.6 J. Positive sign indicates work done by the system. Options A and C are incorrect because the loop is not degenerate, and D is twice the actual area.
